analysis.one_liner: Phases out older oil tank cars, caps crude volatility, and adds rail inspections and first-responder notices.
analysis.headline: The Crude-By-Rail Safety Act was introduced in 2015 with nine Senate sponsors, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: After a series of fiery oil-train derailments, this bill would have banned oil shipments in the older DOT-111 tank cars, capped the volatility (explosiveness) of crude moved by rail, required electronically controlled brakes on long oil trains, and added track inspections, spill-response plans, and notices to local first responders. It also set civil penalties up to $1 million per violation for shippers and railroads that skipped the rules, and $40 million a year for first-responder training and state inspectors. It never got past its committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school along rail lines that carry oil trains, and the local firefighters and emergency crews who respond when one derails. Rail workers also gain from confidential close-call reporting protections.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would immediately prohibit shipping oil in any DOT-111 tank car that does not meet an industry safety circular and in any unjacketed CPC-1232 car, with ethanol shipments in those cars banned two years after enactment.

All new tank cars built after October 1, 2015 would have to meet the toughest design option from the 2014 tank-car rulemaking, and high-hazard flammable trains would have to run with electronically controlled pneumatic brakes.
The Department of Transportation would set a national limit on the volatility of crude oil shipped by rail, with shippers required to spot-test 5% of loaded cars and DOT auditing the results.
Rail carriers would have to run at least two additional internal rail inspections and four track geometry inspections per year on routes carrying high-hazard flammable trains.

Railroads could not run a high-hazard flammable train through a state until they told that state's emergency commission and local planning committees how many trains to expect, what they carry, the routes, and a contact person.
The bill authorizes $40 million a year for fiscal 2016 and 2017 for safety programs including first-responder training and grants to states and communities for inspectors and emergency plans.

Knowing violators would face civil penalties of up to $500,000 per violation, rising to $1 million if a violation causes death, serious injury, or significant environmental damage, and up to $1 million for skipping volatility or rail inspections.

Class I railroads and other covered carriers would have to set up confidential close-call reporting systems, with employees protected from discipline and from related federal enforcement for reports made in the program.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers and shippers, who would bear retrofit, volatility-treatment, testing, and penalty costs, and the large freight railroads, which would bear inspection, braking, disclosure, and reporting costs. Some of that cost would flow into the price of moving crude by rail.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: immediately pulling DOT-111 cars and unjacketed CPC-1232 cars out of oil service, retrofitting the rest to a higher standard, and adding electronically controlled brakes would have cost shippers and railroads substantially, in an industry already short of approved tank cars, and could have raised the cost of moving crude.

A binding volatility limit would have required treating or blending crude before it could be loaded, adding cost and logistics steps for producers of the light, volatile Bakken crude that was then moving heavily by rail.

The bill directs a study of whether a high-hazard flammable train liability regime modeled on the Atomic Energy Act or the vaccine-injury compensation program should apply, which could in a later step shift some catastrophic-accident risk from private insurers and carriers onto a federal framework, an outcome an honest supporter would have to defend on its own terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would have gone to the public: fewer ruptures in derailments, faster and better-informed emergency response, and more trained first responders in towns along oil-train routes. The costs would fall on oil shippers and railroads, concentrated in retrofitting and inspections, and would partly show up in shipping costs. The immediate tank-car ban was aggressive relative to retrofit capacity, but the bill allowed cars that had already been retrofitted to keep running. On balance the design is a straightforward safety regulation whose costs fall on the industries creating the risk.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill and sent it to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on March 25, 2015, joined in the introduction by Senators Baldwin, Feinstein, and Murray.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no markup, vote, or further action is recorded in the action history.
The bill had eight additional cosponsors, seven Democrats and one Independent.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil shippers and freight railroads were better off because the bill never moved: they avoided the retrofit, braking, inspection, testing, and penalty obligations. Communities along oil-train routes kept the pre-existing level of tank-car, volatility, and emergency-response rules.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and no Republican cosponsor or committee action is recorded; the bill died in a Republican-run committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Oil producers and shippers (notably Bakken crude)
industries.note: The bill would have banned their oldest tank cars outright, capped crude volatility, and required 5% spot testing with penalties up to $1 million per violation. Those costs exist precisely because moving volatile crude through towns by rail is the risk the bill targeted; the industry's interest ran against the communities along the routes. The bill dying left shippers with the pre-2015, less costly status quo.

Railroads would have faced extra internal and track-geometry inspections, electronically controlled pneumatic brakes on oil trains, state disclosure duties, a confidential close-call reporting system, and civil penalties. The industry had been fighting the pace of tank-car mandates in the parallel federal rulemaking at the time.

industries.industry: Tank car builders and retrofit shops
industries.note: Requiring all new cars to meet the strictest 2014 design option and retrofitting older cars to keep operating would have created years of guaranteed orders. The industry's gain comes directly from the safety rules the public gets.

Ethanol shipments in DOT-111 and unjacketed CPC-1232 cars would have been prohibited two years after enactment, forcing retrofit or replacement. The same cars also carried ethanol in deadly derailments, so the safety case mirrors the public's.

Stricter operations would reduce accident frequency, but the bill also commissioned a study of whether a federal, nuclear-style liability regime should replace private-market coverage for catastrophic oil-train incidents, which could shrink or reshape that market.
